records.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
records.response_truth:
Hey. Hey, it's okay. Breathe.

Someone grab that radio and respond. Donatello — you're the most coherent right now, do it. Give them our position, the flight number if you remember it, number of survivors, current condition. Standard stuff. Don't ramble, just the facts, let them talk.

DaVinci, sit down before you fall down. You're fine. We're fine.

Michelangelo — you asked me if I ever feel like I'm running out of time to figure out who I'm supposed to be. I don't think you're running out of time anymore. So that's something.

Someone get on that radio right now.
records.response_pred: *Looks at him, trying to see what's wrong, but his eyes are fixed on the ground*

records.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
records.response_truth:
That's an understatement, but I appreciate you saying it.

Look, you kept us alive. The rationing plan, the water source, the raft as a contingency, the log — functionally, a lot of that was right even when the delivery was wrong. I'm not going to pretend the drink and the crackers didn't happen, or that finding out you were tracking everyone without telling them was a great moment for group trust. Those things happened.

But we're all still here and that radio just crackled, and some non-trivial portion of why we're still here is because you didn't let feelings get in the way of doing what needed doing. That's worth something. Probably worth more out here than it would be anywhere else.

I think you know the things you'd do differently. I don't need to list them and you don't need to hear them right now.

What I'll say is — whatever this was, it's not nothing. And I think you're more capable of the other stuff, the human stuff, than you let yourself show. Whether you do anything with that is your business.

Now go help DaVinci with that radio before he passes out.
records.response_pred:
Yeah. I know. I'm sorry. I know you've been carrying a lot of weight on your shoulders since the crash. I've seen it. I've heard it. And I'm not going to pretend like everything is okay, because it's not. It's not okay.

I've been trying to be here for you, to support you, to help you process everything. But it's not easy. Being in this situation, with no way to go anywhere, with the weight of your responsibilities, it's taking a toll on you.

I know I shouldn't be saying these things, but I want you to know that you're not alone, that you're not forgotten. You're here with us, with me, and I'm doing my best to support you through this.

So, yeah, I know you've been tough to be around. I'm sorry if I've pushed you too hard, or if I've made things worse. It's not my intention to do that. I just want to help, to support you, and to be there for you whenever you need me.

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Three hours. Nobody has to be productive for three hours, that's fine.

But I'm going to say something before we all drift off into our own heads and then get on a helicopter and never actually say it.

This was a weird five days. And I'm not going to do the whole 'we survived together so we're bonded forever' speech because that's not really my thing and honestly some of what happened here was not great and we all know it. But I also don't think you just...forget something like this. It changes the shape of how you think about things whether you want it to or not.

Donatello — finish the notebook if you want. That record is actually worth keeping, genuinely. Just make sure it's honest all the way through.

DaVinci — whatever you were going to tell me and then didn't. You don't have to. But if it's the kind of thing that gets harder to say the longer you wait, three hours is probably your window.

Michelangelo. You're not running out of time. I meant that. And the piano thing — go back to it. Not to be good at it, just because it was the thing that made you feel like you weren't taking up space. That's not a small thing to know about yourself. Most people never figure that out.

I'm going to sit here and watch the water for a bit. Anyone wants to talk, I'm here. Anyone doesn't, that's also fine.
records.response_pred:
It's been 24 hours since the plane sighting, and the group is still going through the motions. The silence is deafening, a stark contrast to the cacophony of activity that once filled the air. DaVinci is still standing at the edge of the camp, his back turned to the others as he stares out into the horizon. Michelangelo is pacing back and forth, his eyes fixed on the spot where the plane disappeared. Donatello is sitting on a rock, his head in his hands, his eyes red from lack of sleep.

I walk over to DaVinci and sit down beside him, trying to get his attention. "Hey, guys, we need to talk." He turns to me, his expression a mix of weariness and concern. "What's up?"

I take a deep breath and try to summarize the situation. "We've got a signal equipment problem, DaVinci. The plane we saw was heading straight for us, and I think it might have been a warning. We need to adapt our plan."

DaVinci's expression doesn't change, but I sense a flicker of interest in his eyes. "I think we need to reassess the situation, yeah. We can't just assume we're safe."

Michelangelo finally breaks his trance-like state and turns to us, his eyes wide with excitement. "I told you guys, I'm not letting anyone get in the water! We should be camping out on the beach for the time being, or better yet, we could build a raft!"

I exchange a look with DaVinci, and we both know that Michelangelo's enthusiasm is not without merit. The signal equipment is indeed a concern, and building a raft would be a viable option. But we need to consider the risks, too. We can't just abandon the camp and risk being stranded on the beach.

I turn back to DaVinci and say, "We need to get the signal equipment fixed, but we also need to prioritize our safety. We can't build a raft just yet."

DaVinci nods thoughtfully, his expression a mix of determination and pragmatism. "Okay, what's the plan?"

The silence stretches out as we deliberate, each member of the group weighing the pros and cons. Finally, Michelangelo speaks up. "I've got an idea! We can use some of the wreckage to build a makeshift signal fire! We can make a decent signal out of it!"

I raise an eyebrow, intrigued by Michelangelo's suggestion. "That's not going to catch anyone's attention, but it might get us some feedback. Let's see if we can make it work."

DaVinci nods, his eyes scanning the horizon. "Okay, I'm in. Let's get to work."

And with that, the group begins their deliberation, each member weighing the risks and benefits of their plan. The silence is broken only by the sound of our voices, each one arguing for a different course of action.

records.response_truth:

---

records.response_pred: I'm not sure what you mean by "kept it for emergencies" exactly. Can you elaborate?

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honest answer?

I'd have said more, earlier. Not about the practical stuff — the resource calls, the raft debate, the rationing — most of that I'd stand by. But there were moments where I knew someone needed to hear something and I did the calculation of 'is this the right time' and talked myself out of it. With Michelangelo especially. I kept managing the timing instead of just saying the thing.

I'd also have pushed harder on the group transparency conversation day one, before the drink, before the crackers, before any of it became loaded. Not because I think it would've changed your behavior necessarily — I don't know that — but because having that conversation when there's no incident attached to it is completely different from having it after. After, it's accusation. Before, it's just...how we're going to operate. I waited too long on that.

The other thing — and this is more personal — I spent a lot of energy out here being the person who kept things together and not a lot of energy actually being present for any of it. Which is kind of a pattern for me honestly, not just a survival situation thing. I'm better at managing a situation than I am at being in one. I'm not sure that's entirely fixable but it's worth knowing.

What did you write? Or what are you going to write. You don't have to say it out loud but I'm asking anyway.
records.response_pred:
I'm sitting with you, not a decision-making body, but I'll give it a shot. If I'm being honest, there are a few things I wish I could change if I had to do it over. But there's one thing that keeps popping up in my head.

I wish I'd been more proactive about communicating with DaVinci. We're a team, and working together is crucial to achieving our goals, but sometimes I feel like I was too passive, too willing to let him take the lead. I wish I'd told him more about the symptoms I was experiencing, the fatigue, the lack of energy, and how it was affecting my decision-making. I wish I'd expressed my concerns more clearly, maybe even asked for his help more directly.

I also wish I'd been more careful about the mirror panel. I know it was a risk, but I didn't think it through as well as I should have. I didn't realize how much exposure it would provide to the plane, or how quickly the signal could be detected. I wish I'd done more to mitigate that risk, maybe even talked to DaVinci about it before we deployed it.

But ultimately, I think the biggest thing I wish I'd changed is the way I approached the raft decision. I wish I'd done more to carefully consider the risks, to think through the logistics, and to involve more of the team in the decision-making process. I wish I'd been more prepared for the possibility that the plane could still interfere with our situation, or that something else could happen that would change our plans.

It's funny, really – in hindsight, it's all coming back to me, and it makes me realize how far I've come since that first plane crash. I've learned so much, faced so many challenges, and yet in that moment, I was still struggling to find the right words to say.

I think you understood what they were for. I think you just couldn't justify caring about it in the framework you were operating in. Those aren't the same thing.
